title: A Commentary on the Amitabha Sūtra
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The Amitabha Sūtra is the essential teaching the World-Honored One proclaimed without being asked, the profound sūtra praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions, the wondrous Dharma of ultimate expedience, the supreme and sudden refuge. It is the most important scripture of the Pure Land school, called the first sūtra of the Pure Land, because in it Śākyamuni Buddha reveals the method of liberation that assures rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in this very life.

inline.s: Translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the later Qin dynasty.

The Amitabha Sūtra is the essential teaching the World-Honored One proclaimed without being asked, the profound sūtra praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions, the wondrous Dharma of ultimate expedience, the supreme and sudden refuge. It is the most important scripture of the Pure Land school, called the first sūtra of the Pure Land, because Śākyamuni Buddha here reveals
the method of liberation that assures rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in this very life —
faith, vows, and recitation of the Name, with single-minded, unconfused focus

. Moreover, this Dharma is praised with one voice by the Buddhas of all directions (including, of course, Amitabha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss). Those who deeply give rise to faith and understanding are surely protected and remembered by the Buddhas of all directions; those who practice as taught will certainly be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The sūtra says: "(Among the various)

Buddhas as innumerable as the sands of the Ganges, each in his own land, puts forth his vast and long tongue, covering the entire three-thousand-great-thousand world, and speaks truthful words: You sentient beings should have faith in this sūtra of inconceivable merit, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas."
It also says:

"If there are good men and good women who hear this sūtra and uphold it, and who hear the names of these Buddhas, all these good men and good women will be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas, and will never regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, Śāriputra! You should all believe and accept my words and the words of the Buddhas."

The method of liberation in this life: a way to put an end to birth-and-death and escape the three realms within this very life. Ordinary paths, in order to end birth-and-death and leave the three realms, must completely eradicate all afflictions, which is extremely difficult and almost impossible to attain in one lifetime. But if in this life one cannot put an end to birth-and-death, then because of the confusion of passing from one body to the next, no one knows in which life or kalpa one will again take up the bodhi path. Yet the Buddha-recitation method that the World-Honored One teaches here, so long as one attains single-minded, unconfused focus, will surely bring rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss at death and put an end to birth-and-death. And single-minded, unconfused focus is far easier than eradicating all afflictions; it is something that anyone, with correct method and sincere, persistent effort, can attain in this very life. Therefore "faith, vows, and recitation of the Name, with single-minded, unconfused focus" is a method of liberation in this very life, praised with one voice by the Buddhas of all directions. Those who deeply give rise to faith and understanding are surely gathered in and received by the Buddhas of all directions; those who practice as taught will certainly be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Confusion of passing from one body to the next: forgetting upon being reborn.
In this sūtra, the World-Honored One especially teaches how to ensure rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss:
faith, vows, and recitation of the Name, with single-minded, unconfused focus.

In so doing he establishes the doctrinal framework of the Pure Land school. Therefore this sūtra takes "faith, vows, and recitation of the Name, with single-minded, unconfused focus" as the essential method of practice.

To recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is the most simple, direct, and secure path to escape birth-and-death; and among the four kinds of Buddha-recitation, recitation of the Name is again the most simple, direct, and secure, praised by the ancients as "the shortcut within the shortcut (the shortcut of shortcuts)."

The four kinds of Buddha-recitation: First, recitation of the Name, single-mindedly calling the Buddha's name; second, visualization of the image, gazing upon the Buddha's image while reciting the name; third, contemplation of the mark, inwardly contemplating the Buddha's adorned and splendid marks; fourth, contemplation of true reality, contemplating the true marks of oneself and of all Buddhas, which are neither empty nor existent, both empty and existent, and in which mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are without distinction.

The most distinctive features of this sūtra are: praised by the Buddhas of all directions, protected and remembered by all Buddhas, a horizontal transcendence of birth-and-death, never falling back, and attainment of buddhahood in one lifetime.
Praised by the Buddhas of all directions.
The sūtra says:
(Among the various)

Buddhas as innumerable as the sands of the Ganges, each in his own land, puts forth his vast and long tongue, covering the entire three-thousand-great-thousand world, and speaks truthful words: You sentient beings should have faith in this 'sūtra of inconceivable merit, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas'."
Protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
The sūtra says:

"If there are good men and good women who hear this sūtra and uphold it, and who hear the names of these Buddhas, all these good men and good women will be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas, and will never regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Horizontal transcendence of birth-and-death.
Master Yinguang says:

"Why is chanting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the West called the method of horizontal transcendence? The ancients gave a simile to explain it: they compare ordinary beings, who are replete with delusion and karmic afflictions, to a worm born in the lowest section of a bamboo; and this bamboo stands for the three realms. For this worm to get out there are only two ways: one is vertical emergence, the other horizontal transcendence. Vertical emergence is boring up from below, breaking through each section in turn until the topmost section is broken and only then getting out. This compares to
(the simile)
practicing other methods, which require eradicating all affliction of views and thought before one can escape the three realms
(before one can leave the three realms and put an end to birth-and-death)

. Afflictions of view number eighty-eight kinds, and afflictions of thought number eighty-one grades, and so many grades are compared to the sections of a bamboo. The worm boring straight upward is called vertical emergence. For example, a sage of the first fruit, who has cut off the afflictions of view, must undergo seven lifetimes in the heavens and seven in the human world through long kalpas of practice before attaining arhatship and ending birth-and-death. The second fruit must likewise pass one life in the heavens and return once to the human world before reaching the fourth fruit. As for the third fruit, whose afflictions of thought in the desire realm are already exhausted, one must still gradually practice in the five heavens of No-Return before eradicating the afflictions of thought and attaining the fourth fruit. Only then is one counted a sage beyond instruction who has escaped the three realms. If one is of dull faculties at the third fruit, one must even be reborn in the four heavens of emptiness, ascending from the heaven of the infinity of space to the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception, before attaining the fourth fruit. This method of vertical emergence is thus arduous and long. Horizontal transcendence, on the other hand, is this worm not breaking upward through each section but boring a single hole sideways, and so coming out. Such a method is far easier than vertical emergence. Those who chant the Buddha's name are likewise. Though they have not eradicated the afflictions of view and thought
(the afflictions of view and thought)

, if they can be complete in the three provisions of the Pure Land — faith, vows, and practice — at the moment of death they can move Amitabha Buddha to come and guide them to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once there, in that pure land, the afflictions of view and thought are eradicated without being eradicated. Why? Because the land of the Pure Land is excellent and its conditions are strong, with no conditions that give rise to affliction. Thus one gains the three non-regressions, and continues on until one pierces the dust-like
(the dust-mote afflictions)
ignorance
(the afflictions of ignorance)
, and perfects the supreme bodhi
(attaining buddhahood)

. How direct and simple a matter this is! Therefore the ancients said: pursuing the Way through other gates is like an ant climbing a tall mountain; chanting the Buddha's name for rebirth is like a sailboat driven by a favoring breeze."
(From a Dharma talk given upon returning from Shanghai to Lingyan)

The three realms: the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The desire realm is the world of sentient beings who have the two desires of sexual appetite and food, including from the six heavens of desire above, through humans and animals, down to the hungry ghosts and hells. The form realm is the world of sentient beings who are free of the two desires of sexual appetite and food but still have a body of form, including the eighteen heavens of the four dhyānas. The formless realm is the world of sentient beings who have no physical body but abide in mind-consciousness in deep and wondrous concentration, including the four heavens of emptiness (the heaven of the infinity of space, the heaven of the infinity of consciousness, the heaven of nothingness, and the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception). These three realms are all realms in which ordinary beings transmigrate in birth-and-death, so Buddhist practitioners first take escape from the three realms as their goal.
The three non-regressions:

First, non-regression of position, in which the position attained through practice is not lost; second, non-regression of practice, in which the method one practices is not lost; third, non-regression of mindfulness, in which correct mindfulness does not regress. Afflictions of view and thought: the afflictions of views and the afflictions of thought. Afflictions of views are the delusions and errors of ordinary beings in regard to views, such as the five wrong views of self-view, extreme view, wrong view, view of attachment to views, and view of attachment to precepts and practices. Afflictions of thought are the delusions and errors of ordinary beings in regard to thought, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, ignorance, pride, and doubt. These two afflictions are the root cause of sentient beings falling into the three realms and suffering birth-and-death in vain; to cut them off is to be able to end birth-and-death and escape the three realms. The dust-mote afflictions: these are the afflictions of bodhisattvas. When bodhisattvas work to convert sentient beings, if they do not penetrate the countless dharmas as numerous as dust and sand, they cannot complete the work of teaching sentient beings — hence the name dust-mote afflictions. The afflictions of ignorance: these are fundamental ignorance, which obscures the true principle of the middle way; when completely eradicated, one becomes a Buddha.
Never falling back.
The sūtra says:
"Sentient beings born in the land of Ultimate Bliss are all avinivartaniya
(never regressing)
Attaining buddhahood in one lifetime.
The sūtra says:
"All these good men and good women will be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas, and will never regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi
(no longer regressing, until the attainment of buddhahood)

The Amitabha Sūtra has two extant translations: one is The Sūtra of the Buddha's Teaching on Amitabha, translated by Master Kumārajīva in the Yao-Qin period, often called the Qin translation; the other is The Sūtra of Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha's Protection and Reception, translated by Master Xuanzang in the Tang dynasty, often called the Tang translation. Master Kumārajīva, responding to the disposition of his countrymen to prize conciseness, translated mainly for meaning, so the text is concise yet rich, exquisite and fluent. Master Xuanzang, in order to preserve the original as much as possible, translated word for word literally, accurate and complete, retaining the original terms with precise and detailed meanings, which avoids the faults of misinterpretation and fabrication — and this is crucial for study and practice. When studying the sūtra deeply, comparing the two translations against each other yields a deeper and more accurate understanding. For the commentary on the Tang translation, see
A Commentary on the Sūtra of Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha's Protection and Reception
Note: the headings in this text were added by the commentator and do not belong to the sūtra itself.

blocks.text: 1. The Fine Assembly of the Buddha's Companions

inline.s: Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at the Garden of the Benefactor of Orphans and the Trees of Jeta in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, together with a great assembly of monks numbering twelve hundred and fifty, all of whom were great arhats, well known to all.

This is what I (Ānanda) personally heard. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha was at the Garden of the Benefactor of Orphans and the Trees of Jeta in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, together with a great assembly of monks numbering twelve hundred and fifty, all of whom were great arhats well known to all.

Thus have I heard: this is what I (Ānanda) personally heard. This sūtra was recited by Ānanda, a disciple of Śākyamuni Buddha, when the scriptures were compiled. Ānanda: his full name is Ānanda, one of the ten great disciples of the Buddha. He was the Buddha's cousin, born on the night when the Buddha attained the Way; later he left home under the Buddha and attended him for twenty-five years, serving as the Buddha's attendant. He was renowned as foremost in extensive learning, and many scriptures were recited by him at the compiling. The ten great disciples: the ten great disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha, namely: Śāriputra, foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana, foremost in supernatural powers; Subhūti, foremost in understanding emptiness; Ānanda, foremost in extensive learning; Upāli, foremost in upholding the precepts; Aniruddha, foremost in the divine eye; Mahākāśyapa, foremost in the ascetic practice; Pūrṇa, foremost in teaching Dharma; Kātyāyana, foremost in debate; Rāhula, foremost in secret practice. The ascetic practice: the practice of casting aside the three attachments of robes, food, and dwelling. One who cultivates the ascetic practice must observe twelve rules, called the "twelve ascetic practices." At one time: at that time. Śrāvastī: the name of an ancient kingdom in central India, also transliterated as Sāvatthi, located in what is now northwestern India, on the southern bank of the Rapti River. The Garden of the Benefactor of Orphans and the Trees of Jeta: this is a garden in Śrāvastī where Śākyamuni Buddha expounded this sūtra. Monk: one who has left home and received full ordination; a man is called a bhikṣu, a woman a bhikṣuṇī. Great monks: an expression describing that these monks were all of high attainment. Together: all gathered. Well known to all: known to everyone.
