Led by these great arhats were: the elder Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Revata, Cūḍapanthaka, Nanda, Ānanda, Rāhula, Gavāṃpati, Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja, Kālodayin, Mahākapphina, Bakkula, Aniruddha, and all these great disciples.

The elder Śāriputra: "elder" means a monk of years and high virtue; "Śāriputra" is one of the ten great disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha, renowned as foremost in wisdom. Mahā: a Sanskrit sound, translated in Chinese as great. Mahāmaudgalyāyana: that is, the great Maudgalyāyana, "great" added to distinguish him from another disciple surnamed Maudgalyāyana.
And likewise the great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: Mañjuśrī, the Prince of Dharma, Ajita Bodhisattva, Gandhahastī
(qián)
Bodhisattva, and Nitya-praśānta Bodhisattva, together with all these great bodhisattvas.
There were also all the great bodhisattvas: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Gandhahastī Bodhisattva, and Nitya-praśānta Bodhisattva, together with all these great bodhisattvas.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattva: a Sanskrit sound, translated in Chinese as great bodhisattva. Mañjuśrī, the Prince of Dharma: that is, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. Ajita Bodhisattva: that is, Maitreya Bodhisattva.
And likewise Śakra, lord of the gods, together with the countless gods of all the heavens.
And also Śakra and the countless gods of all the heavens came to the assembly.
Śakra, lord of the gods: also called Indra, lord of the second heaven (the heaven of the Thirty-three).

blocks.text: (1) What Is Meant by Ultimate Bliss

inline.s: At that time the Buddha said to the elder Śāriputra: To the west from here, passing through a hundred thousand koṭīs of Buddha-lands, there is a world called the Land of Ultimate Bliss. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitabha, who is now preaching the Dharma. Śāriputra! Why is that land called the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Because the sentient beings of that nation are free from all suffering and experience only happiness — therefore it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

At that time, the Buddha told the elder Śāriputra: from here toward the west, passing through a hundred thousand koṭīs of Buddha-lands, there is a world called the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The Buddha of that world is named Amitabha, who is now preaching the Dharma. Śāriputra! Why is that Buddha-land called the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Because the sentient beings there are free from all suffering and have only all manner of happiness — therefore it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Buddha-land: the territory over which a single Buddha teaches. Sentient beings: here it means all living beings. World-Honored One: an honorific title for the Buddha, because the Buddha is honored by all people in the world.

blocks.text: (2) The Splendor of the Dependent Retribution

inline.s: Dependent retribution: the karmic reward upon which sentient beings dwell, such as the land, the earth, buildings, and furnishings — that is, the environment of one's life.

Furthermore, Śāriputra! In the land of Ultimate Bliss there are seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of netting, and seven tiers of trees, all made of the four treasures, and wholly surrounding it — therefore that land is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Furthermore, Śāriputra! In the land of Ultimate Bliss, everywhere are seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of netting, and seven tiers of trees, surrounding it on all sides. They are all made of the four treasures, exquisitely beautiful — therefore that land is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Railings: balustrades. "Railing" refers to the horizontal rail; "shǔn (
shǔn/dùn

)" refers to the vertical rail. Netting: the netting of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with gold threads, pearls, and a hundred thousand varied gems, with jeweled bells hanging on all four sides, radiant in color and splendor, spread over the jeweled trees. The jeweled nets emit light, and within the light appear the images of the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; whichever land one thinks of in the mind appears of itself accordingly. Rows of trees: trees arranged in ordered rows.
Seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of netting, seven tiers of trees:
the railings surround the trees, and the exquisite jeweled nets cover the trees, layer upon layer alternating, their number being seven. The Sūtra of the Immeasurable Life of the Buddha says:

"Immeasurable jeweled nets spread over the Buddha-land, all made of gold threads, true pearls, and a hundred thousand varied gems, wondrous and rare, adorned and embellished, hanging jeweled bells on all four sides, radiant in color and dazzling, utterly magnificent. A naturally virtuous breeze arises softly and stirs gently. That breeze is harmonious, neither cold nor hot, mild and soft, neither slow nor swift. It blows through the jeweled nets and the many jeweled trees, producing immeasurable subtle sounds of Dharma, spreading a hundred thousand kinds of gentle and fragrant virtue. Those who hear them — their dust of toil and habits of defilement naturally do not arise. When the wind touches their bodies, they all gain bliss, like a monk who attains the concentration of cessation."
The four treasures: gold treasure, silver treasure, vaidūrya treasure, and sphatika treasure. Surrounding it on all sides: "circuit," to go around; making one full circuit is called one "circuit."

Furthermore, Śāriputra! In the land of Ultimate Bliss there are ponds of seven treasures, filled with water of eight qualities of merit, and the bottom of the ponds is entirely laid with golden sand. On the four sides are steps and paths, made of gold, silver, vaidūrya, and crystal. Above are pavilions and towers, also adorned with gold, silver, vaidūrya, crystal, conch-shell, red pearls, and agate. In the ponds are lotus flowers as large as carriage wheels, blue ones radiating blue light, yellow ones radiating yellow light, red ones radiating red light, and white ones radiating white light — subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure. Śāriputra! The land of Ultimate Bliss perfects such adornments of merit.

Furthermore, Śāriputra! In the land of Ultimate Bliss there are ponds of seven treasures, filled with water of eight qualities of merit, and the bottom of the ponds is entirely laid with golden sand. On the four sides are steps and paths, all made of gold, silver, vaidūrya, and crystal. Above are pavilions and towers, also luxuriously adorned with gold, silver, vaidūrya, crystal, conch-shell, red pearls, and agate. In the seven-treasure ponds, the lotus flowers are as large as carriage wheels; blue lotus flowers radiate blue light, yellow lotus flowers radiate yellow light, red lotus flowers radiate red light, and white lotus flowers radiate white light — subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure. Śāriputra! The land of Ultimate Bliss perfects such splendid, gorgeous, and wondrous merit.

Water of eight qualities of merit: this water has eight qualities — clear and pure, cool and refreshing, sweet and delicious, light and soft, moistening, serene and harmonious, allaying hunger and thirst, and nourishing all the faculties. Vaidūrya: a treasure like jade but translucent. Conch-shell (chē qú): according to the Expanded Materia Medica, Volume Forty-six, the conch is a large clam of the sea, with ridged markings on its shell like the tracks of a carriage wheel on the ground; the interior of its shell is white and smooth as jade, so it is often mistaken for jade. Later generations mostly use white coral and shells to make things called conch-shell. Red pearls: red precious jewels, exceedingly rare and precious. Adornments of merit: such splendid, gorgeous, and wondrous merit.

Furthermore, Śāriputra! In that Buddha-land heavenly music is always playing, the ground is made of gold, and in the six periods of the day and night mandārava flowers rain down. The sentient beings of that land, at dawn, each take up fine flowers in their robes, and go to make offerings to a hundred thousand koṭīs of Buddhas in the other directions. At the time of the midday meal they return to their own land, and eat and walk, and so on. Śāriputra! The land of Ultimate Bliss perfects such adornments of merit.

Furthermore, Śāriputra! That Buddha-land always has harmonious, elegant, and wondrous heavenly music, the ground is made of gold, and in the six periods of the day and night, mandārava flowers fall as though like rain. The sentient beings there, at early morning, each take up various fine flowers in their robes, and go to make offerings to a hundred thousand koṭīs of Buddhas in the other directions. At the time of the morning meal (breakfast), they return to their own land, and then eat, walk in meditation, and so on. Śāriputra! The land of Ultimate Bliss perfects such splendid, gorgeous, and wondrous merit.

The six periods of the day and night: ancient India divided a day and night into six periods: early day, middle day, late day, early night, middle night, and late night. Raining mandārava flowers: raining heavenly mandārava flowers as though from the sky; "flower" is the old word for "flower." Robe-jū (
gāi
): the lower hem of a long robe. Offering: the meaning of presenting and honoring. Meal: to eat; here "meal" is used as a verb. In the Sūtra of the Immeasurable Life it describes it thus:

"When one wishes to eat, bowls of seven treasures naturally appear before one. Gold, silver, vaidūrya, conch-shell, agate, coral, amber, moonstones, true pearls — such bowls come of their own accord. A hundred flavors of fine food naturally fill them. Though there is this food, there is in fact no one who eats; one only sees the forms and smells the fragrance, and conceives of it as food, and is naturally satisfied. Body and mind become soft and at ease, with no clinging to flavor; the matter passes away, and when the time comes it appears again."

Walking meditation: walking in a circle round a fixed place, cultivating concentration in the midst of movement. In this way one cultivates both motion and stillness, adjusting body and mind, and also avoids the dullness or drowsiness that comes from sitting long. Eating and walking meditation: the text speaks only of eating and walking, which is an abbreviated expression, "eating" standing for the activities of life and "walking meditation" for the deeds of practice.

Moreover, Śāriputra! In that land there are always all kinds of wondrous birds of various colors: white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śāris, kalaviṅkas, and two-headed birds. These many birds, in the six periods of the day and night, produce harmonious and elegant sounds, and their sounds proclaim the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and such dharmas. When the sentient beings of that land hear these sounds, they all recollect the Buddha, recollect the Dharma, and recollect the Saṃgha.

Moreover, Śāriputra! In the land of Ultimate Bliss there are always all kinds of wondrous, brightly colored birds: white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śāris, kalaviṅkas, and two-headed birds. These many birds, in the six periods of the day and night, produce harmonious and elegant sounds, proclaiming the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and such dharmas. When the sentient beings of that land hear these sounds of Dharma, they all single-mindedly recollect the Buddha, recollect the Dharma, and recollect the Saṃgha.

The two-headed bird: a bird with one body and two heads. The five faculties: the faculty of faith, the faculty of effort (also called the faculty of diligence), the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. "Faculty" means root or foundation; these five faculties are the roots from which all wholesome dharmas grow. The five powers: the power of faith, the power of effort (also called the power of diligence), the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. When the five faculties gradually grow, they produce power — this is the five powers. The seven factors of enlightenment: "enlightenment" is bodhi; the "seven factors of enlightenment" are seven kinds of awakening: choosing the Dharma (the ability to choose the true Dharma), effort, joy (the joy that arises on attaining wholesome dharmas), tranquility, mindfulness (maintaining right mindfulness), and concentration. The seven factors of enlightenment are obtained through the five faculties and the five powers. The eightfold noble path: the eightfold noble path is also called the "eight right paths," a method of practice made up of eight mutually related parts: First, right view, which is correct understanding. Second, right thought, which is correct thinking. Third, right speech, which is proper words. Fourth, right action, which is proper conduct. Fifth, right livelihood, which is a proper occupation or way of life. Sixth, right effort, which is proper exertion. Seventh, right mindfulness, which is correct recollection. Eighth, right concentration, which is correct meditation. This method of practice is sacred because anyone who walks this noble path will surely become a noble one, distancing himself from suffering and affliction and passing beyond birth-and-death.

Śāriputra! Do not think that these birds are actually born as retribution for offenses. Why? Because in that Buddha-land there are no three evil destinies. Śāriputra! In that Buddha-land there is not even the name of evil destinies, how much less the reality? These many birds are all transformations made by Amitabha Buddha, in order to let the sounds of Dharma flow forth.

Śāriputra! Do not think that these birds are all born as retribution for offenses. Why? Because the Land of Ultimate Bliss has no three evil destinies. Śāriputra! In the Land of Ultimate Bliss there is not even the name of evil destinies — how could there really be beings of evil destinies? These many birds are all transformations Amitabha Buddha made by his power, in order to let the sounds of Dharma flow forth, and they have no consciousness.

The three evil destinies: the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals. These are the lower three destinies among the six destinies (hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and gods). Sentient beings, from beginningless time, transmigrate within these six destinies.

Śāriputra! In that Buddha-land, the gentle wind moves the various jeweled trees and the jeweled nets, producing subtle and wondrous sounds, as if a hundred thousand kinds of music were all playing at once. Those who hear these sounds naturally all give rise to the mind of recollecting the Buddha, recollecting the Dharma, and recollecting the Saṃgha. Śāriputra! The land of Ultimate Bliss perfects such adornments of merit.

Śāriputra! In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the gentle wind moves the various jeweled trees and the jeweled nets, producing subtle and wondrous sounds, as if a hundred thousand kinds of music were being played at the same time. Hearing these beautiful sounds, one naturally gives rise to the mind of recollecting the Buddha, recollecting the Dharma, and recollecting the Saṃgha. Śāriputra! The land of Ultimate Bliss perfects such splendid, gorgeous, and wondrous merit.

blocks.text: (3) The Splendor of the Proper Retribution

inline.s: Proper retribution: the bodies and minds of Buddhas and sentient beings; this is the proper karmic reward obtained in accordance with past karmic causes.

Śāriputra! What do you think? For what reason is that Buddha named Amitabha? Śāriputra! The light of that Buddha is immeasurable, illuminating the lands of the ten directions without obstruction — therefore he is called Amitabha. Furthermore, Śāriputra! The lifespan of that Buddha and of his people is immeasurably, boundlessly many asaṃkhyeya kalpas — therefore he is called Amitabha.

Śāriputra! How do you conceive of it? For what reason is the Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss called Amitabha? Śāriputra! The light of that Buddha is immeasurable, illuminating the lands of the ten directions without obstruction — therefore he is called Amitabha. Furthermore, Śāriputra! The lifespan of that Buddha and of his people is immeasurably, boundlessly many asaṃkhyeya kalpas — therefore he is called Amitabha.

What do you think: how do you conceive of it? Amitabha: translated in Chinese as immeasurable. This is because the Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss has immeasurable light, and the lifespan of that Buddha and his people is also immeasurable — therefore he is called the Buddha of Immeasurable Light (Amitabha Buddha). The lifespan of that Buddha and of his people, immeasurably, boundlessly many asaṃkhyeya kalpas: the lifespan of Amitabha Buddha and his people is immeasurably, countlessly many great kalpas. The Tang translation says:
"Śāriputra, because that Tathāgata and the sentient beings there have a lifespan of immeasurable, countless great kalpas."
An asaṃkhyeya
(qí)
kalpa: translated in Chinese as a kalpa of countless number. Countless: without end.

Śāriputra! Since Amitabha Buddha attained buddhahood, it is now ten kalpas. Furthermore, Śāriputra! That Buddha has immeasurable, boundless śrāvaka disciples, all arhats, whose number cannot be known by reckoning; the multitude of bodhisattvas is likewise. Śāriputra! That Buddha-land perfects such adornments of merit.

Śāriputra! Since Amitabha Buddha attained buddhahood, it is now ten kalpas. Furthermore, Śāriputra! Amitabha Buddha has immeasurable, boundless śrāvaka disciples, all arhats, whose number cannot be known by reckoning; and Amitabha Buddha's bodhisattva disciples are likewise, immeasurable and boundless, beyond the knowledge of reckoning. Śāriputra! That Buddha-land perfects such splendid, gorgeous, and wondrous merit.

Śrāvaka: one of the ten dharma-realms (hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas). An arhat is the highest fruit among the śrāvaka realm. Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas are called the four noble paths, no longer transmigrating in birth-and-death. Beyond the knowledge of reckoning: this cannot be known by counting.
Question: Are there women in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West?
Answer: There are no women in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West. The Sūtra of the Buddha's Teaching on the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Awakening (a Chinese translation) says:
"In that land
(the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West)
are all bodhisattvas and arhats; there are no women, and their lifespans are extremely long, without number of kalpas. Women who are reborn there are transformed and born all as men."
The Sūtra of the Buddha's Teaching on Amitabha's Three Kinds of Buddha, the Wonderful Dharma and the Path Across the Realm of Humans says:

"The second vow: when I attain buddhahood, let there be no women in my land. Women who wish to come and be born in my land will be born as men. The countless gods and humans, and the winged and creeping creatures of every kind, who come to be born in my land, are all transformed and born within the lotus flowers of the seven-treasure ponds. When grown they all become bodhisattvas and arhats, all without number. Only upon attaining this vow will I become a Buddha; if I do not attain this vow, in the end I will not become a Buddha."
Bodhisattva Vasubandhu's Treatise on Rebirth says:
"In the realm of Mahāyāna roots, there is no name even of reproach: women, the handicapped, and the two-vehicle species are not born there; whatever beings rejoice in, everything can be fulfilled."
Master Yinguang says:
"The Land of Ultimate Bliss has no women. Women, and animals, born in that world are all in the form of young men, born by transformation in the lotus."
(From the Collected Letters of Master Yinguang, Third Compilation
Letter One to the Layman Ye Fubei)

Furthermore, Śāriputra! Those born in the land of Ultimate Bliss are all avinivartaniya (never regressing); among them many are bodhisattvas of one more birth, their number exceedingly great, beyond the knowledge of reckoning — it can only be expressed as immeasurable, boundless asaṃkhyeyas.

Moreover, Sariputra! The sentient beings born into that Land of Ultimate Bliss are all avivartika (non-retrogressive), and many among them are bodhisattvas of one-life-completing, whose number is so great that it cannot be known by calculation, but can only be spoken of as immeasurable, boundless, and innumerable.
[Avi-
(pi)

-vartika] Sanskrit; rendered into Chinese as non-retrogressive. This means that after being born into the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one only advances stage by stage until Buddhahood, and never retrogresses. [One-life-completing] In this one lifetime one can fill the Buddha-position; this is an alternate name for the bodhisattva of the final body (the bodhisattva of equal enlightenment).

[Bodhisattva of equal enlightenment] The fifty-first among the fifty-two stages, the bodhisattva who is about to realize the Buddha-fruit; his merit and wisdom are nearly equal to the Buddha’s, and so he is called “of equal enlightenment.” For example, Avalokitesvara, Mahasthamaprapta, and Maitreya are all bodhisattvas of equal enlightenment. [Fifty-two stages] From an ordinary being to Buddhahood, a bodhisattva must pass through fifty-two stages: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment. [Wondrous enlightenment] Enlightening oneself and enlightening others, with the practice of enlightenment completely fulfilled, and wisdom and virtue inconceivable, this is called “wondrous enlightenment”; it is the unexcelled right enlightenment of the Buddha-fruit, and one who realizes this right enlightenment is called a “Buddha.”

Question: When a sentient being is born into the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, he has no more birth and death, and becomes a Buddha in one lifetime. Why then does it say here that the bodhisattva of one-life-completing is one “who in this one lifetime can fill the Buddha-position”?

Answer: There are two kinds of birth and death: segmental birth and death, and transformational birth and death. When it is said that “a sentient being born into the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss has no more birth and death, and becomes a Buddha in one lifetime,” the one lifetime refers to one lifetime within segmental birth and death; while when it is said that “the bodhisattva of one-life-completing is one who in this one lifetime can fill the Buddha-position,” the one lifetime refers to one lifetime within transformational birth and death.

[Segmental birth and death] The sentient beings of the three realms and six destinies, because they are recompensed by good and evil karma, all have their lifespans limited and their bodies sectioned, and so their birth and death are called “segmental birth and death.” One who has ended segmental birth and death escapes the cycle and leaves the three realms. [Transformational birth and death] The sages of the three vehicles (the voice-hearer, the solitary-realizer, and the bodhisattva vehicles) have already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and ended segmental birth and death. In the course of the Way, deluded thoughts gradually perish while realization gradually increases; this shift of delusion and realization differs from one period to the next. The passage from a previous period into a later one is exactly like a single birth and death, and its change is wondrous, subtle, and unfathomable, beyond thought, and so it is called “transformational birth and death.” One who has ended transformational birth and death fully realizes the Buddha-fruit.

[Sariputra! All who hear this should make the vow, “I wish to be born in that land.” Why is this so? Because then they will be able to associate with such excellent people, who all gather in the same place.]

Sariputra! When sentient beings hear of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they should all make the vow, “I wish to be born in that land.” Why is this so? Because then they will be able to gather together with such a multitude of bodhisattvas of one-life-completing.
To be able to gather together with such a multitude of bodhisattvas of one-life-completing—what wonderful fellowship, and what unsurpassed conditions for study and practice is this

[Such excellent people] These are not merely good among human beings, but the good among the good, and so they are called excellent people. “Such excellent people” refers to the multitude of bodhisattvas of one-life-completing spoken of above.
[Sariputra! It is not by a small stock of virtue, merit, and karmic conditions that one can be born in that land.]
Sariputra! It is not by lacking the karmic condition of virtue and merit that one is born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Good roots] The good of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind; because they can produce wonderful fruits, they are called good roots. [The good of the three karmas of body (conduct), speech, and mind] Not to kill, not to steal, and not to commit sexual misconduct—this is good of body; not to speak falsely, not to speak divisively, not to speak harshly, and not to speak idly—this is good of speech; not to be greedy, not to be angry, and not to be deluded—this is good of mind. [Merit] The blessing recompensed by cultivating good conduct. [It is not by a small stock of virtue and merit, ’s karmic conditions that one can be born in that land.]
The Tang translation says:
“It is not sentient beings of small good roots who shall be reborn in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitayus.”
[Sentient beings] Also called living beings, that is, all creatures endowed with consciousness.
In the Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha says:
“Those who wish to be born in that land
(the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)

should cultivate the three kinds of merit: first, to honor and support one’s parents, to serve one’s teachers and elders, to be compassionate and not kill, and to cultivate the ten wholesome deeds; second, to receive and uphold the three refuges, to fulfill all the precepts, and not to violate the dignified deportment; third, to arouse the bodhi-mind, deeply to believe in cause and effect, to recite the Mahayana, and to encourage those who practice.”
Therefore, those who recite the Buddha’s name must reverently cultivate the three meritorious practices of the Pure Land, so as to possess the karmic conditions of abundant virtue and merit.

[Ten wholesome deeds] The ten wholesome karmas: not to kill, not to steal, not to commit sexual misconduct, not to speak falsely, not to speak divisively (not to stir up quarrels), not to speak harshly (not to use cutting, abusive words), not to speak idly (not to speak meaningless words), not to be greedy, not to be angry, and not to be deluded (not to act contrary to right principle). See
An Explanation of the Ten Wholesome Karma Paths

. [Three refuges] The three refuges: taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Sangha. This is taking refuge in the three jewels: the Buddhas are the Buddha-jewel, the right Dharma is the Dharma-jewel, and the noble sangha is the Sangha-jewel. [Arousing the bodhi-mind] Arousing the great mind that seeks the Buddha-way above (attaining Buddhahood) and saves sentient beings below.
The Buddha’s teaching of the three studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom—the precepts are the foundation of concentration,
and those who recite the Buddha’s name should strictly uphold the five precepts and the ten wholesome deeds in order to increase their virtuous roots and merit

, and to lay a firm foundation. If one lacks virtuous roots and merit, one will constantly be deluded by the objects of the senses and entangled by karmic hindrances, and “the ten thoughts succeeding one another, accumulating habits until they become a second nature” will be hard to bring about. Therefore the Buddha, in the Amitabha Sutra, especially points out:
“It is not by a small stock of virtue, merit, and karmic conditions that one can be born in that land.”
In the Sutra of Immeasurable Life the Buddha says:
“You should decide for yourselves,
make your bodies upright and your conduct correct,
and further do many good deeds.
Cultivate yourselves and purify your bodies,
washing away the defilement of the mind.
Let words and actions be faithful and sincere, outward and inward in accord. If one can save oneself and then rescue and help others in turn, earnestly seeking the vow,
accumulating the roots of goodness.
Though one toils for a single lifetime, in a brief moment, one will be born in the land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss unending.”

[Five precepts] Not to kill, not to steal, not to commit sexual misconduct, not to speak falsely, and not to drink intoxicants. Not to kill is not to take the life of a living creature; not to steal is not to take another’s property; not to commit sexual misconduct is to do nothing contrary to the marriage bond; not to speak falsely is not to tell deceitful lies; and not to drink intoxicants is not to consume drink or drugs that stupefy the mind.
Therefore, while earnestly reciting the Buddha’s name (the primary practice), one must also put an end to evil and do good (the auxiliary practice) in order to remove the obstacles on the path.
Master Yinguang said:

“Single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and at the same time cultivate worldly good as an auxiliary practice, following the method of Yongming and Lianchi, and there is nothing at which one will not succeed. One should reform one’s own evil and cultivate good, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name. All one’s relatives, old friends, and those with whom one has karmic ties should also be taught in this way.”
(Reply to a letter from Resident Scholar of Yongjia, the sixth; he also said:)

“As for the method of practice, only the recitation of the Buddha’s name is the foremost, and therefore one should focus mainly on faith, vows, and recitation of the name. Then, adding ‘commit no evil, practice all that is good’ as an auxiliary practice, the benefit is great indeed.”
(Reply to a letter from Resident Scholar Fang Shengzhao, the sixth.)
[Doing good] To do charitable deeds is certainly doing good, but the most important doing good is still doing the good of one’s own three karmas of body, speech, and mind (

not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, not speaking divisively, not speaking harshly, not speaking idly, not being greedy, not being angry, not being deluded
). Therefore, doing good chiefly means doing the good of one’s own three karmas of body, speech, and mind. Master Shandao, an incarnation of Amitabha Buddha, set us a brilliant example:
“Guarding the precepts, not violating them in the least.”

(See the Record of the Sages of the Pure Land.) It is a pity that some doctrines nowadays broadly label the cutting off of evil and doing good as “mixed practice,” and set the conduct of the precepts in opposition to the recitation of the Buddha’s name, and even loudly proclaim that one need not cut off evil and do good, and that to do evil for a whole lifetime is of no account, because the evil person is the very object that Amitabha Buddha saves. (See
The Original-Vow Teaching Is a Teaching Mounted on the Buddha
.) [Conduct of precepts] The practice of guarding the precepts.
In
the Online Buddhist Academy of Renshuo Xixing’s
“Pure Practice”

course schedule, the first stage is precisely “cutting off evil and doing good.” Through the study of this first stage’s courses one comes to understand the principle, the methods, and the practical steps of cutting off evil and doing good, and so can make the cutting off of evil and doing good more systematic, more thorough, and more solid.

At the same time, one should also cultivate the four immeasurable minds of kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, and apply them in daily life, to remove suffering and give joy, without resentment, without vexation, without anger, without hatred.

[Four immeasurable minds] The immeasurable mind of kindness, the immeasurable mind of compassion, the immeasurable mind of joy, and the immeasurable mind of equanimity. To give joy to all sentient beings is called the immeasurable mind of kindness; to remove the suffering of all sentient beings is called the immeasurable mind of compassion; to see others doing good, or freed from suffering and gaining joy, and to be filled with delight, is called the immeasurable mind of joy; and to let go of the above three minds without clinging to them, treating friend and foe alike, arousing neither affection nor aversion, is called the immeasurable mind of equanimity. Because these four minds universally connect with countless sentient beings and draw forth immeasurable merit, they are called the immeasurable minds.
Question: I too realize that cutting off evil and doing good is the foundation of Pure Land practice, but I find it hard to begin. What should I do?
Answer: On the question of where to begin in cutting off evil and doing good, I would especially recommend to you a short essay:
The Record of Yu Jingyi’s Encounter with the Kitchen-God (Original and Plain Speech)
(for the notes, see
The Notes on the Record of Yu Jingyi’s Encounter with the Kitchen-God

), which is a model example of reforming one’s destiny. I hope you will read it over and over, ponder it, grasp it, and put it into practice. Of these, the step of practice is especially important; only through continual practice can one realize the true meaning of the essay, and indeed the repeated reading, pondering, and grasping are all for the sake of practice. If time permits, it would be best to follow
the Online Buddhist Academy of Renshuo Xixing’s
“Pure Practice”
course schedule, and to systematically study the five courses of the first stage, “cutting off evil and doing good.” Likewise, in this course of study the practical step remains the center.
It must be pointed out that the World-Honored One emphasized especially in the sutra:
“It is not sentient beings of small good roots who shall be reborn in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitayus.”

But the Original-Vow teaching loudly proclaims: to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss one “need not cut off evil and do good,” “need not uphold the precepts,” “doing evil and committing crimes is of no account,” “the evil person is the very object Amitabha Buddha saves,” “reciting the name one is certainly reborn,” “the gate of the great vow,” and so on (see
the essay “The Original-Vow Teaching Is a Teaching Mounted on the Buddha”

). This is nothing less than leading people toward a pit of fire, preaching in a manner directly opposed to the Buddha. The believers deluded by them neither earnestly recite the Buddha’s name (they were perfectly able to recite earnestly, but being deluded by them into thinking that “reciting the name one is certainly reborn,” they become careless and no longer recite earnestly), nor do they cut off evil, do good, and cultivate the ten wholesome deeds; indeed, some, emboldened (believing that “the evil person is the very object Amitabha saves”), recklessly do evil. The result is that not only are they not reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, but at death, drawn by their evil karma, they fall into the three evil destinies (hells, hungry ghosts, animals), unable to keep even a human body.

The function of cutting off evil, doing good, and upholding the precepts is: first, to tame the mind; second, to increase merit; third, to remove karmic hindrances. If one who recites the Buddha’s name neither cuts off evil and does good nor upholds the precepts, with a mind like a runaway horse or a mad elephant, how can he fix the mind in one place and attain the single-minded recollection without confusion? Merit is a help on the bodhi-way, while karmic hindrances are an obstacle. When merit (the help) is greater than karmic hindrances (the obstacle), what should be done, one is moved to do, and does it energetically and with enjoyment; what should not be done, one does not do, and can resolutely put down; at the end of life, the star of merit shines high, aiding rebirth. But when karmic hindrances (the obstacle) are greater than merit (the help), what should be done, one has no desire to do, and even if one forces oneself, one does it listlessly, doing little and stopping much; what should not be done, one does energetically and with enjoyment, tirelessly; and at the end of life, karmic hindrances appear and obstruct rebirth.

For example, knowing full well that “if the ten thoughts at the end of life succeed one another, one is reborn,” the foremost, most important matter for the reciter of the Buddha’s name is to recite the Buddha’s name at all times and in all places with ten thoughts succeeding one another, so that the habit becomes a second nature. Therefore, through all the hours of the day, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one should never let go of the ten succeeding thoughts; this is the great peace, the great liberation of the wise. Yet many who recite the Buddha’s name cannot do it. In truth, “through all the hours of the day, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, never letting go of the ten succeeding thoughts” is no harder than going to work, and being reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss surpasses becoming a billionaire by countless times! Why can they not “never let go of the ten succeeding thoughts,” yet for the sake of a little profit can suffer every grievance and toil day and night? The reason is that they are blocked by karma (analyze yourself, observe others, and you will understand how karma hinders). Therefore the Buddha here especially instructs:
“It is not by a small stock of virtue, merit, and karmic conditions that one can be born in that land.”

[Sariputra! If a good man or a good woman hears of Amitabha Buddha, and upholds his name, for one day, for two days, for three days, for four days, for five days, for six days, for seven days, with a single-minded mind unconfused; then when that person comes to the end of life, Amitabha Buddha, with the holy assembly, appears before him; and at that very moment, his mind undeluded, he is reborn in the Amitabha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss.]

Sariputra! If a good man or a good woman hears of Amitabha Buddha, and upholds his name, for one day, for two days, for three days, for four days, for five days, for six days, for seven days, attaining a single-minded mind unconfused; then when that person comes to the end of life, Amitabha Buddha, with the holy assembly, appears before him, in compassion and grace extends protection so that his mind is not confused, and he is reborn in the Amitabha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Good man] The Buddha calls a man who cultivates the five precepts and the ten wholesome deeds a good man. [Good woman] The Buddha calls a woman who cultivates the five precepts and the ten wholesome deeds a good woman. [Single-minded mind unconfused] The thought of reciting the Buddha is clear and distinct, neither dull nor scattered. As to what a single-minded mind unconfused is, Master Ouyi teaches:
“The single-mindedness in affairs
(the single-minded mind unconfused in affairs)
is that the thought is clear and distinct, neither dull nor scattered.”
(The Complete Works of Lingfeng
Middle dot
Occasional Talks in the Brahma Chamber.)
Regarding this passage of scripture, the eighth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Lianchi, teaches:

“This speaks of the recitation of the name. The Amitabha Sutra says: ‘When one hears of Amitabha Buddha and upholds his name, for one day, two days, up to seven days, with a single-minded mind unconfused. Then when that person comes to the end of life, Amitabha Buddha, with the holy assembly, appears before him. At that time his mind, unconfused, is reborn in the Amitabha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss.’ This is the recitation of the name for ten thousand ages
from which it issues,
the great source,
, and is personally proclaimed by the golden mouth
the wondrous Dharma
indeed
(The Collected Sayings of Yunqi on the Pure Land.)

Master Lianchi’s teaching here means: this passage on a single-minded mind unconfused is the fundamental basis (the great source from which it issues) for the recitation of the name for ten thousand ages, and is the wondrous Dharma of rebirth personally proclaimed by the golden mouth of the World-Honored One. Therefore, those who recite the Buddha’s name must strictly follow this passage in their practice, so as to ensure rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
As for what it is to correctly uphold the name,
the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Chewu, teaches:
“That which is called upholding the name means to clasp it to one’s breast with firm devotion
, that is, to hold it fast in the mind and never for a moment forget it.
If there is the least interruption of a single thought
(the thought of recitation being interrupted by a wandering thought)
, then it is no longer upholding. If there is the least admixture of a single thought
(the least admixture of a wandering thought)
, then it is no longer upholding. When thought after thought succeeds without admixture or interruption, that is true diligence.
With diligence unceasing,
one gradually enters the single-minded mind unconfused
, and fully accomplishes the Pure Land practice.”
(The Collected Works of Master Chewu.)
[Classp it to one’s breast with firm devotion (
ying

)] “Classp it to one’s breast”: to hold firmly and not let go, extended to mean earnest; “firm devotion”: to bear it in mind fervently. “Clasp it to one’s breast with firm devotion” describes earnestly bearing in mind without forgetting.
Question: What are the single-mindedness in affairs and the single-mindedness in principle?

Answer: The single-mindedness in affairs and the single-mindedness in principle are also called the mind unconfused in affairs and the mind unconfused in principle. The recitation of the name has a holding in affairs and a holding in principle. The holding in affairs is to recite Amitabha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; the holding in principle is to recite the self-nature Buddha (the Amitabha of self-nature). The holding in affairs is urgent for rebirth; the holding in principle aims at seeing one’s nature.
Master Ouyi says: “

The single-mindedness in affairs is that the thought is clear and distinct, neither dull nor scattered; the single-mindedness in principle is to accord quietly with the unborn, and to illumine clearly one’s self-nature.
” (The Complete Works of Lingfeng
Middle dot Occasional Talks in the Brahma Chamber.)
(See
the essay “Single-Mindedness in Affairs and Single-Mindedness in Principle”
Question: Does the “clear and distinct” spoken of above mean that the Buddha-name should be recited very clearly?

Answer: That is not the meaning. “Clear and distinct” means this: the Buddha-name being recited should be clear and distinct in the mind (each sentence of the Buddha-name is clearly known in the mind).
Question: What does “neither dull nor scattered” mean?

Answer: “Neither dull nor scattered” means: neither dullness nor scatteredness. That is, if a wandering thought arises, know it and do not follow it, not be thrown into confusion by it. Therefore, the single-minded mind unconfused in recitation does not mean that not one wandering thought arises, but that one is not deluded by wandering thoughts, and does not let wandering thoughts succeed one another into a train of thought. In short, one is not thrown into confusion by wandering thoughts. Of course, this is only the most elementary requirement of a single-minded mind unconfused; making further effort upon this foundation, one will reach the realm where there is no wandering thought in thought after thought, and the Buddha-name is a single, pure field.
Question: The sutra says:
“For one day, for two days, for three days, for four days, for five days, for six days, for seven days, with a single-minded mind unconfused.”
Within a single day, even within seven days, can one truly attain a single-minded mind unconfused?

Answer: “For one day up to seven days” is an enumerative phrase, an abridged expression. The detailed expression, for example, is what the World-Honored One said in the Great Discourse on the Application of Mindfulness:
“Bhikkhus! Anyone who, in this way, rightly cultivates the four applications of mindfulness
for seven years
, may expect one of two fruits: either the highest wisdom in this very life
(realizing the fruit of arhatship)
, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of non-return
(realizing the fruit of anagami).
Bhikkhus!
Let alone seven years
Bhikkhus!
Let alone six years
Bhikkhus!
Let alone one year
Bhikkhus!
Let alone seven months
Bhikkhus!
Let alone one month
Bhikkhus!
Let alone half a month
, if anyone, in this way, rightly cultivates the four applications of mindfulness
for seven days,
may expect one of two fruits: either the highest wisdom in this very life, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of non-return.”

[Four fruits] Cultivating the four noble truths has four fruits: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-return, and the fruit of arhatship. Among them, the fourth fruit, the arhat, is the highest; one who reaches this fruit is released from birth and death and receives no further becoming.

As for the question “within a single day, even within seven days, can one attain a single-minded mind unconfused,” the answer is: the single-minded mind unconfused in recitation is the realm of the ten thousand thoughts returning to the One, and the ten thousand thoughts returning to the One is only the most elementary realm of practice. For the Chan school, one must pass through the ten thousand thoughts returning to the One, and the One returning to nothing, and so clarify the mind and see one’s nature
, and then do the work of guarding, until the delusions of views and thoughts are entirely cut off, only then can one end birth and death and escape the cycle

. Therefore, some Chan practitioners have already had the ten thousand thoughts return to the One, but are still quite far from clarifying the mind and seeing their nature; once they hear of the supreme excellence of the Pure Land teaching and turn to recitation, they can attain a single-minded mind unconfused in recitation within a single day, even within seven days. Since ancient times such examples have been too numerous to list singly; see the Record of the Sages of the Pure Land. And Chan practitioners who have already clarified the mind and seen their nature, turning to cultivate the Pure Land teaching, can within a single day attain a single-minded mind unconfused in recitation, and many afterwards became masters and virtues of the Pure Land school; see the Record of the Sages of the Pure Land. For example, Master Chewu, who was the thirty-sixth patriarch of the Linji school, broadened the lecture platform and led the assembly in Chan, spurring on later students with tireless delight. Fourteen years as one day, his fame spread through the south and north, and the linage spirit was greatly revived. But later, whenever he recalled Master Yongming (the sixth Pure Land patriarch), a master of the Chan lineage, who nonetheless set his heart on the Pure Land and recited the Buddha’s name a hundred thousand times a day, longing to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; and how much more, in this age of the Dharma’s end, should one follow the legacy of Master Yongming. So he left the Chan monastery and practiced exclusively the Pure Land, teaching countless beings, and became the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school.

As for those who study the Buddha’s teaching who have not generally yet attained the returning of the ten thousand thoughts to the One, the time will be somewhat longer; how long it will take depends on each person’s foundation and progress. Generally speaking, as long as the method is correct (for example, cultivating according to
Awareness of Recitation (Concise Edition)

), through diligent effort everyone can attain the single-minded mind unconfused in recitation. This matter requires self-confidence (profound faith that one can attain the single-minded mind unconfused), constancy, and perseverance. That self-confidence, constancy, and perseverance can change one’s destiny, Yu Jingyi set us an excellent example; see
The Record of Yu Jingyi’s Encounter with the Kitchen-God (Original and Plain Speech)
(for the notes, see
The Notes on the Record of Yu Jingyi’s Encounter with the Kitchen-God

Therefore, those who recite the Buddha’s name must have true faith and sincere vows, and be diligent without respite. Though one toils for a lifetime, it is but a moment; and once one reaches the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one’s lifespan is immeasurable, bliss is unending, and one becomes a Buddha and saves sentient beings, fulfilling the great vow of bodhi.
Question: How does one attain a single-minded mind unconfused?
Answer: See
the essay “How to Attain a Single-Minded Mind Unconfused”
Question: The Praise of the Buddha’s Reception Sutra says:

“For one day and night, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven, with the thought bound without confusion. When that good man or good woman comes to the end of life, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, together with his countless disciples and the assembly of bodhisattvas, surrounded front and back, comes and stands before him,
and in compassion and grace extends protection, so that his mind is not confused.
Having given up his life, he follows the Buddha’s assembly and is born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Immeasurable Life.”

Since one has already attained the thought bound without confusion (the single-minded mind unconfused), why does it then speak of Amitabha’s coming and, after his coming, “in compassion and grace extending protection, so that his mind is not confused”?

Answer: The thought bound without confusion (the single-minded mind unconfused) is the cause that draws the Buddha to come welcome, but the thought bound without confusion is a shallow-level practice, often insufficient to maintain the mind unconfused at the moment when the four elements decompose, suffering presses in, and demons manifest. Therefore Amitabha’s “in compassion and grace extending protection, so that the mind is not confused” ensures rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The Sutra of Praising the Merit of the Buddhas says:
“When one’s life is about to end, with a single mind of faith and joy, the thought not forgotten and not abandoned
this is the right thought at the end of life, drawing the Buddha to come welcome
, Amitabha Buddha will
(lead)
the many assembled monks
(the assembly of disciples and bodhisattvas)
and stand before him; and the demons will at last be unable to destroy
(this good man or woman’s)
mind of right enlightenment.”

Here, “the demons will at last be unable to destroy their mind of right enlightenment” is precisely because of Amitabha’s “in compassion and grace extending protection, so that the mind is not confused.”
[Sariputra! I see this benefit, and therefore speak these words. If there are sentient beings who hear these words, they should make the vow, “I wish to be born in that land.”]

Sariputra! I see such supreme benefit, and therefore speak these words (that upholding the name with a single-minded mind unconfused assures rebirth). If there are sentient beings who hear this message that upholding the name with a single-minded mind unconfused assures rebirth, they should make the vow, and cultivate as is taught, to be born in that land.
The Tang translation says:

“Sariputra! I, observing such great matter of benefit and peace, speak these truthful words: if any pure-hearted good man or good woman, having heard of such inconceivable merit of the name of the Buddha Immeasurable Life, and of the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, should believe, accept, and make the vow,
and cultivate as taught,
he is born in that Buddha-land.”
[Therefore I speak these words] These words are:

“If a good man or a good woman hears of Amitabha Buddha, and upholds his name, for one day, for two days, for three days, for four days, for five days, for six days, for seven days, with a single-minded mind unconfused; then when that person comes to the end of life, Amitabha Buddha, with the holy assembly, appears before him; and at that very moment, his mind undeluded, he is reborn in the Amitabha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss.”

The vow here is made after the World-Honored One has told of the certain rebirth of one who upholds the name with a single-minded mind unconfused, and then immediately says: “I see this benefit, and therefore speak these words. If there are sentient beings who hear these words, they should make the vow, ‘I wish to be born in that land.’” Therefore, the vow here is the vow of “upholding the name with a single-minded mind unconfused,” so as to ensure rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

blocks.text: 5. The Buddhas of the Various Quarters Praise

inline.s: [Sariputra! Just as I now praise the inconceivable virtue and benefit of Amitabha Buddha, so too in the east there are the Buddhas Akshobhya
chu
Bhe
pi

Buddha, Sumeru-form Buddha, Great Sumeru Buddha, Sumeru-light Buddha, and Wondrous-sound Buddha; and such Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each in his own land puts forth the broad and long tongue, covering the whole three-thousand-great-thousand world, and speaks these truthful words: “You sentient beings shall believe in this sutra that praises inconceivable virtue and is protected and kept in mind by all the Buddhas.”]

Sariputra! Just as I now praise the inconceivable virtue and benefit of Amitabha Buddha, so too in the east there are Akshobhya Buddha, Sumeru-form Buddha, Great Sumeru Buddha, Sumeru-light Buddha, and Wondrous-sound Buddha, and such Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each in his own land puts forth the broad and long tongue, and speaks these truthful words to the entire three-thousand-great-thousand world he teaches: “You sentient beings should all believe and accept this sutra that praises the inconceivable virtue of Amitabha Buddha and is protected and kept in mind by all the Buddhas.”

[Broad and long tongue] One of the Buddha’s thirty-two marks: the Buddha’s tongue is broad and long, soft, red, and thin, able to cover the face up to the hairline. With such a tongue, his speech is necessarily true. [Covering the whole three-thousand great-thousand world, speaking words of truth] To the whole three-thousand great-thousand world that he teaches, he speaks words of truth. [Three-thousand great-thousand world] That is, a great-thousand world, which is the region that a single Buddha teaches. One Mount Sumeru together with the four great continents is called a small world. A collection of one thousand small worlds is called a “small-thousand world”; a collection of one thousand small-thousand worlds is called a “middle-thousand world”; a collection of one thousand middle-thousand worlds is called a “great-thousand world.” Because it reckons by thousands three times, a great-thousand world is also called a “three-thousand great-thousand world.” [A sūtra protected and recollected by all Buddhas] This Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Amitabha Buddha is protected and recollected by all Buddhas. The passage below explains:

“Why is it called the sūtra protected and recollected by all Buddhas? Sāriputra! If virtuous men or virtuous women hear this sūtra and uphold it, and hear the names of all the Buddhas, these virtuous men and women are all protected and recollected by all the Buddhas, and all attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.”

[Sāriputra! In the southern world there are the Buddha Sun-Moon-Lamp, the Buddha Renowned Light, the Buddha Great-Blaze-Shoulder, the Buddha Sumeru-Lamp, the Buddha Immeasurable Diligence, and so on, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each in his own land puts forth the broad and long tongue, covering the whole three-thousand great-thousand world, and speaks words of truth: “You sentient beings should believe in this sūtra that praises the inconceivable merit and virtue and is protected and recollected by all Buddhas.”]

Sāriputra! In the southern world there are the Buddha Sun-Moon-Lamp, the Buddha Renowned Light, the Buddha Great-Blaze-Shoulder, the Buddha Sumeru-Lamp, the Buddha Immeasurable Diligence, and so on, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each in his own land puts forth the broad and long tongue, and to the whole three-thousand great-thousand world that he teaches speaks words of truth: You sentient beings should all believe in and accept this sūtra that praises the inconceivable merit and virtue of Amitabha Buddha and is protected and recollected by all Buddhas.
[Sāriputra! In the western world there are the Buddha Immeasurable Life, the Buddha Immeasurable Marks, the Buddha Immeasurable Banner
chuáng

, the Buddha Great Light, the Buddha Great Radiance, the Buddha Jeweled Marks, the Buddha Pure Light, and so on, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each in his own land puts forth the broad and long tongue, covering the whole three-thousand great-thousand world, and speaks words of truth: “You sentient beings should believe in this sūtra that praises the inconceivable merit and virtue and is protected and recollected by all Buddhas.”]

Sāriputra! In the western world there are the Buddha Immeasurable Life, the Buddha Immeasurable Marks, the Buddha Immeasurable Banner, the Buddha Great Light, the Buddha Great Radiance, the Buddha Jeweled Marks, the Buddha Pure Light, and so on, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each in his own land puts forth the broad and long tongue, and to the whole three-thousand great-thousand world that he teaches speaks words of truth: You sentient beings should all believe in and accept this sūtra that praises the inconceivable merit and virtue of Amitabha Buddha and is protected and recollected by all Buddhas.

[Sāriputra! In the northern world there are the Buddha Blaze-Shoulder, the Buddha Supreme Sound, the Buddha Hard-to-Overcome, the Buddha Sun-Born, the Buddha Net-of-Light, and so on, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each in his own land puts forth the broad and long tongue, covering the whole three-thousand great-thousand world, and speaks words of truth: “You sentient beings should believe in this sūtra that praises the inconceivable merit and virtue and is protected and recollected by all Buddhas.”]

Sāriputra! In the northern world there are the Buddha Blaze-Shoulder, the Buddha Supreme Sound, the Buddha Hard-to-Overcome, the Buddha Sun-Born, the Buddha Net-of-Light, and so on, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each in his own land puts forth the broad and long tongue, and to the whole three-thousand great-thousand world that he teaches speaks words of truth: You sentient beings should all believe in and accept this sūtra that praises the inconceivable merit and virtue of Amitabha Buddha and is protected and recollected by all Buddhas.

[Sāriputra! In the world below there are the Buddha Lion, the Buddha Renowned, the Buddha Renowned-Light, the Buddha Dharma, the Buddha Dharma-Banner, the Buddha Upholding-Dharma, and so on, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each in his own land puts forth the broad and long tongue, covering the whole three-thousand great-thousand world, and speaks words of truth: “You sentient beings should believe in this sūtra that praises the inconceivable merit and virtue and is protected and recollected by all Buddhas.”]

Sāriputra! In the world below there are the Buddha Lion, the Buddha Renowned, the Buddha Renowned-Light, the Buddha Dharma, the Buddha Dharma-Banner, the Buddha Upholding-Dharma, and so on, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each in his own land puts forth the broad and long tongue, and to the whole three-thousand great-thousand world that he teaches speaks words of truth: You sentient beings should all believe in and accept this sūtra that praises the inconceivable merit and virtue of Amitabha Buddha and is protected and recollected by all Buddhas.

[Sāriputra! In the world above there are the Buddha Brahma-Sound, the Buddha Star-King, the Buddha Supreme-Fragrance, the Buddha Fragrance-Light, the Buddha Great-Blaze-Shoulder, the Buddha Adorned with Assorted Jewelled Flowers, the Buddha King of the Sal Trees, the Buddha Jewelled Flower Virtue, the Buddha Who Sees the Meaning of All Things, the Buddha Like Mount Sumeru, and so on, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each in his own land puts forth the broad and long tongue, covering the whole three-thousand great-thousand world, and speaks words of truth: “You sentient beings should believe in this sūtra that praises the inconceivable merit and virtue and is protected and recollected by all Buddhas.”]

Sāriputra! In the world above there are the Buddha Brahma-Sound, the Buddha Star-King, the Buddha Supreme-Fragrance, the Buddha Fragrance-Light, the Buddha Great-Blaze-Shoulder, the Buddha Adorned with Assorted Jewelled Flowers, the Buddha King of the Sal Trees, the Buddha Jewelled Flower Virtue, the Buddha Who Sees the Meaning of All Things, the Buddha Like Mount Sumeru, and so on, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each in his own land puts forth the broad and long tongue, and to the whole three-thousand great-thousand world that he teaches speaks words of truth: You sentient beings should all believe in and accept this sūtra that praises the inconceivable merit and virtue of Amitabha Buddha and is protected and recollected by all Buddhas.

[Sāriputra! What do you think? Why is it called the sūtra protected and recollected by all Buddhas? Sāriputra! If virtuous men or virtuous women hear this sūtra and uphold it, and hear the names of all the Buddhas, these virtuous men and virtuous women are all protected and recollected by all the Buddhas, and all attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.]

Sāriputra! What do you think? Why is this sūtra called the sūtra protected and recollected by all Buddhas? Sāriputra! If virtuous men or virtuous women hear this sūtra and believe in and accept it, and practice in accordance with it, and also hear the names of all the Buddhas, these virtuous men and women are all protected and recollected by all the Buddhas, and no longer retrogress from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (the stage of Buddhahood).

[One who hears this sūtra and upholds it] “Receive” means to believe and accept; “uphold” means to act in accordance with the scripture. “One who hears this sūtra and upholds it” is one who believes in and accepts this sūtra and practices in accordance with it. [The Chinese transliteration a-nou (
nòu
)-duo-luo-san-miao (
miǎo

)-san-puti] Sanskrit transliteration. Translated into Chinese it means: the supreme, correct, and equal enlightenment. An arhat attains correct enlightenment; a bodhisattva attains correct and equal enlightenment; a Buddha attains the supreme, correct, and equal enlightenment.
The Tang translation says:

“Sāriputra, if virtuous men or virtuous women have already heard, or will hear, or now hear this sūtra and, having heard it, deeply give rise to faith and understanding. Having given rise to faith and understanding, they must surely be received and taken in by the World-Honored Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges rivers, dwelling in the ten directions.
Those who practice as taught
, all are certain to be non-retrogressing from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and all are certain to be reborn in the pure Buddha land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Immeasurable Life Buddha.”
[Jingjia (
jìng jiā

)] A Sanskrit transliteration of “Ganges.” [Those who practice as taught: all are certain to be non-retrogressing from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi] Those who practice as taught are all certain never to retrogress, advancing from the higher to the highest, until they attain Buddhahood.
[Therefore, Sāriputra! You should all believe in and accept my words, and what the Buddhas have said.]
Therefore, Sāriputra! You should all believe in and accept what I have said and what the Buddhas above have said; practice as taught, and harbor no doubt.
The Tang translation says:
“Therefore, Sāriputra, you sentient beings should all believe in, accept, and understand the words of me and of the World-Honored Buddhas of the ten directions; diligently and earnestly
practice as taught, and harbor no doubt

[Sāriputra! If there are people who have made the vow, who now make the vow, or who will make the vow, desiring to be reborn in the land of Amitabha Buddha, these people all attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi in that land — whether they have already been reborn, are now reborn, or will be reborn.]

Sāriputra! If there are people who have already made the vow, now make the vow, or will make the vow (establishing the vow to uphold the Name and attain one mind undisturbed), desiring to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, they are all certainly able to go, and there, without retrogressing, practice to Buddhahood — whether they have already been reborn, are now reborn, or will be reborn.
[Making the vow] Establishing a vow.
The Tang translation says:

“Sāriputra, if virtuous men or virtuous women, regarding the merit, virtue, and adornment of the pure Buddha land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Immeasurable Life, have already made the vow, will make the vow, or now make the vow, they must surely be received and taken in by the World-Honored Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges rivers, dwelling in the ten directions.
Those who practice as taught
, all are certain to be non-retrogressing from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and all are certain to be reborn in the pure Buddha land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Immeasurable Life Buddha.”
[Therefore, Sāriputra! If virtuous men and virtuous women have faith, they should make the vow, that they may be reborn in that land.]
Therefore, Sāriputra! If virtuous men and virtuous women have faith, they should make the vow to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The Tang translation says:

“Therefore, Sāriputra, if virtuous men or virtuous women of pure faith, all should, regarding the pure Buddha land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Immeasurable Life, with deep mind believe and understand, make the vow and be reborn,
and not practice laxity
[Do not practice laxity] Never give oneself up to indulgent ease; diligently and without slack, practice as taught.

[Sāriputra! As I now praise the inconceivable merit and virtue of the Buddhas, those Buddhas in turn praise my inconceivable merit and virtue, saying: Śākyamuni Buddha is able to do an exceedingly difficult and rare thing! In the Sahā land, in the evil world of the five turbidities (the turbidity of the eon, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of life), he attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and for the sake of sentient beings speaks this Dharma that is hard to believe in all the world.]

Sāriputra! As I now praise the inconceivable merit and virtue of the Buddhas, those Buddhas in turn praise my inconceivable merit and virtue, saying: Śākyamuni Buddha is able to do an exceedingly difficult and rare thing! In the evil world of the five turbidities (the turbidity of the eon, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of life) of the Sahā land, he realizes Buddhahood, and for the sake of sentient beings speaks this Dharma that is hard to believe in all the world.
[Sahā (
suō

)-land] “Sahā” is Sanskrit transliteration. Translated into Chinese it means “Capable of Enduring” (kanren). It means that the sentient beings of this land are content in the ten evils, endure the three poisons and all afflictions, and are unwilling to leave and get out; hence it is called the World of Endurance (the Sahā world), or in short the Land of Endurance. [The turbidity of the eon, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of life] The turbidity of the eon: born in a degenerate age, war, famine, plague and the like arise one after another, the people suffer unspeakably, and there is never a day of peace. The turbidity of views: people’s views are not correct, they do not revere the true Way, and diverse teachings abound, with no one reaching agreement. The turbidity of afflictions: people are greedy for love and pleasure, wrathful and contentious, endlessly false and deceitful. The turbidity of sentient beings: people are for the most part corrupt and evil, body and mind impure, and fail to grasp principle. The turbidity of life: because afflictions gather thickly, body and mind are worn out, and life is short. [The Dharma hard to believe] The Land of Ultimate Bliss is so supreme that, once one attains one mind undisturbed, one can rely on the Buddha’s power and be reborn there, attaining Buddhahood in a single lifetime. But how many people in the world truly believe and practice as taught? Therefore this is a Dharma hard to believe in the world.

[Sāriputra! Know that I, in the evil world of the five turbidities, did this difficult thing — attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and spoke this hard-to-believe Dharma for all the world — this is exceedingly difficult!]

Sāriputra! You should know that I, in the evil world of the five turbidities, did this difficult thing — realized Buddhahood and spoke this hard-to-believe Dharma for all the world — this is truly exceedingly difficult!

[When the Buddha had spoken this sūtra, Sāriputra and the monks, all the devas, humans, asuras and others of the world, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully believed and accepted it, and made obeisance and departed.]

When the Buddha had proclaimed this sūtra, Sāriputra and the monks, all the devas, humans, asuras and others of the world, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully believed and accepted it, and made obeisance and departed.

[Deva] One of the six destinies, the one with the most excellent retribution among the six, with a very long lifespan and a life of felicity. [Six destinies] Hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas. [Asura] One of the six destinies; translated into Chinese it means “not a deva,” because they have the bliss of devas and humans but not their virtue — like devas, yet not devas. In their former lives they too were quite willing to cultivate merit, but their envy and hatred were very heavy, and so they turned and were reborn in the asura destiny. [Samsara] Sentient beings, from the beginningless past, transmigrate through birth and death within the six destinies, turning like a wheel without cease.
